records.issue_text: match_count read-modify-write in should_block? is unsynchronized; concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose increments — should use update_all with match_count = match_count + 1
records.rationale: In `app/models/blocked_email.rb` `should_block?` performs a read-modify-write on `match_count` (`record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`). Under concurrent calls for the same `email`, two threads/processes can read the same `match_count` and both write back `+1`, losing an increment. This is a real race that can cause inaccurate statistics (`match_count`, `last_match_at`) and should be done atomically (e.g., `update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or `increment_counter`).
records.stripped_text: match_count read-modify-write in should_block? is unsynchronized; concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose increments — should use update_all with match_count = match_count + 1

records.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the new `rejectedEmails` mechanism returns a validation failure with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` when an email is in the rejected list (added on server error via `rejectedEmails.pushObject(result.values.email)`). records.issue_text: No case normalization on blocked email storage or lookup, allowing the blocklist to be bypassed by case variations of the blocked address
records.rationale: Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive with no normalization: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` and the validator passes the raw `value` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`). There’s no `downcase`/canonicalization in the model, validator, or migration, so storing `Bad@spam.com` and signing up with `bad@spam.com` (or vice versa) can bypass the block. The unique index on `:email` also won’t prevent case variants in common DBs (e.g., Postgres).
